Foundations: Choosing Your Digital Income Model and Getting Work-Ready

There is more than one way to earn online, and each one pays, grows and fails differently. This module helps you choose the model that fits your skills and life, then prepares your data, power, device and working hours so that clients in Lagos, London or New York can rely on you.
Four ways to earn online: remote job, freelancing, e-commerce and digital products
Describe the four main digital income models and how money flows in each
Compare the models on income stability, control, start-up cost and skills needed
Match your own skills and circumstances to one model to start with
Recognise income-model promises that are unrealistic

People say 'make money online' as if it were one thing. It is not. There are **four different models**, and the daily work, the way money arrives and the risks are very different in each. Choosing the right one for this season of your life saves you months of effort in the wrong direction.
A woman working on a laptop with a world map behind her
Digital work lets your skill travel even when you stay at home, but each income model travels differently.
Model 1: the remote job

A **remote job** is employment where you work for one organisation from home. You have a manager, set duties, and a fixed monthly salary or a fixed contract fee. Examples include customer support agent, virtual assistant on a part-time contract, social media coordinator, data entry clerk or online tutor for a tutoring company. The big advantage is **predictable income**. The trade-off is less control: the employer sets your hours, your tasks and often your tools. Competition for remote roles is strong because applicants can come from many countries.
Model 2: freelancing

A **freelancer** sells a defined service to several clients, project by project or on a monthly retainer. A retainer is a fixed monthly fee for an agreed amount of ongoing work. A freelancer might write blog posts, design flyers, manage Instagram pages or transcribe audio. You choose your clients and prices, but income goes up and down, and you must find the work yourself. If you choose this model, the WODDI Institute course Freelancing Fundamentals goes deeper into packaging and pricing.
Model 3: e-commerce

**E-commerce** means selling physical goods online: shea butter, ankara bags, baked snacks, children's clothes. The selling happens on WhatsApp catalogues, Instagram, Facebook Marketplace, Jumia or your own simple website, but the product is real and must be stored, packed and delivered. You need money for stock, and your profit depends on cost price, delivery and returns. The internet widens your market; it does not remove the work of a shop.
Model 4: digital products

A **digital product** is something you make once and sell many times as a file or access: a budget spreadsheet template, a recipe e-book, a set of Canva templates for church programmes, a recorded short course. There is no stock and no delivery cost. The catch: sales usually start slowly, because people must first trust you and find you. Digital products work best for someone who already has an audience or teaching ability.

Ngozi, for example, is a 38-year-old secondary school teacher in Enugu with two children. She has strong English, uses Google Docs well and can spare about 15 hours a week, mostly evenings and Saturdays.
She lists her skills: clear writing, explaining things simply, organising documents.

Ngozi starts with one model that fits her hours and skills, and keeps a second model as a planned next step rather than trying all four at once.
Promises that should make you stop

Be careful with offers that promise large, fixed daily earnings for 'simple online tasks', ask you to pay a registration or 'activation' fee before you can work, or pay you to recruit other people. Real employers and real clients pay you; they do not charge you to start. Task and recruitment schemes of this kind have cost many Nigerians their savings.

Whichever model you pick, three things stay the same: you need a **skill someone will pay for**, a **reliable way to work online**, and **trust**, which you build through clear communication and keeping your promises. The rest of this course works on all three, with a focus on the standards that remote clients and employers expect.

Your work-ready setup: device, data, power and a backup plan
List the minimum device and software needs for your chosen digital work
Measure your own data use and build a monthly data budget

Set up simple file backup so work is never lost

A client abroad does not see NEPA, network outages or a dead phone battery. They only see that your work arrived late or your call dropped. In Nigeria, a **backup plan for power and internet** is part of being professional, not an extra. This lesson helps you build a setup you can trust on the days that matter.
A woman working at a desk at home with a laptop
A small, reliable home setup with backups is worth more than an expensive device that fails on deadline day.
Device: what you actually need

Match the device to the work. Many tasks can start on a good **smartphone**: customer support on WhatsApp, social media management, simple Canva designs, transcription with earphones. A **laptop** becomes necessary for long documents, spreadsheets, heavy design, coding or any job that needs two windows open at once. Before buying, check the job requirement. Many remote job adverts state the minimum, for example a laptop with a webcam and a headset.
**Headset or earphones with a microphone**: they cut background noise on calls far more than a better phone does.
**Free office tools**: Google Docs, Sheets and Drive work in a browser or as phone apps.
**Up-to-date software**: install updates, because they fix security holes.
**A screen lock and a separate work email** so personal and client matters stay apart.
Data: measure, then budget

Guessing your data use leads to running out in the middle of a client call. Instead, **measure it**. On Android, open Settings and look for Network or Data usage; on iPhone, open Settings then Mobile Data. Note how much each app used over one normal work week. Video calls and uploading large files use the most. Turning your camera off on calls, and downloading files on Wi-Fi when you can, both save data.

Also stop data leaks you do not need. Turn off automatic video play in social apps, set WhatsApp media to download on Wi-Fi only, and stop phone backups from running over mobile data. Treat work data as a **business cost**: write it in your records each month like rent or transport, because it comes out of what you earn.
Worked example: a monthly data budget
Amina, for example, does social media management for two small businesses from Kano. She checks her phone's data usage screen after one ordinary work week.
Her phone shows that work apps used 3.2 GB that week: Instagram and Facebook 1.8 GB, Google Meet 0.9 GB, WhatsApp 0.3 GB, Google Drive 0.2 GB.
Four weeks of the same work: 3.2 GB x 4 = 12.8 GB.
She adds about 25% as a safety margin for extra calls and uploads: 12.8 GB x 1.25 = 16 GB.
She compares data plans from two networks and chooses a plan of at least 16 GB that suits her budget, writing the price down as approximate because plans change often.
She keeps a small top-up on her second SIM for emergencies.
Amina knows she needs about 16 GB a month for work and budgets for it as a business cost, instead of running out in week three.
Power and internet backups
**Charge everything the night before** important calls and deadlines: phone, laptop, power bank.
**Keep a power bank** big enough to charge your phone at least once. For laptops, know where you can work if light goes off, such as a hub, office or a friend's place with an inverter.
**Use two SIMs from different networks.** When one network is weak in your area, switch the hotspot to the other.
**Work offline when you can.** In Google Docs, turn on offline access so you can keep typing without internet; it will sync later.
**Tell clients early** if a known problem is coming, such as a planned outage or travel.
Deadline-day backup plan
Main internet fails
Switch to second SIM
Still down: work offline
Message client before deadline
Deliver once connected
Each step has a fallback, and the client hears from you before the deadline, not after it.
Never lose work: simple backups

Save client work in a **cloud folder** such as Google Drive, not only on your phone. If your phone is stolen or your laptop breaks, the files are safe. Use clear names, for example 'ClientName_Instagram-plan_2026-03_v2', so you and the client can always tell which version is the latest. Keep one folder per client, with sub-folders such as 'Briefs', 'Drafts' and 'Final'. Once a month, check that your phone's photos and documents are also backing up, because a client voice note or screenshot you need as proof can be lost with the phone. Turn on **2-Step Verification** for the Google account that holds client files, so a stolen password alone cannot open them.
Electricity safety at home

Use a surge protector or stabiliser for laptops and chargers, because power often returns with a surge. Do not overload one extension socket, keep cables away from water and from where children walk, and switch off and unplug equipment during heavy lightning storms.

Working across time zones and setting your availability
Convert times between West Africa Time, UK time and US Eastern time, including seasonal changes
Find the overlap hours between you and a client abroad
Write clear availability and response-time statements

When you work with clients outside Nigeria, time becomes a skill. A meeting at '3pm' means nothing until you know **whose 3pm**. Missing a call because of a time-zone mistake is one of the fastest ways to lose a new client, and it is completely avoidable.
A person looking at an online calendar with scheduled events
Putting every client meeting in a calendar with the correct time zone prevents most scheduling mistakes.
The time zones you will meet most

Nigeria uses **West Africa Time (WAT)**, which is **UTC+1** all year. UTC is the world's reference time. Nigeria does not change its clocks. Many client countries do. The **United Kingdom** uses GMT (UTC+0) in winter and British Summer Time (UTC+1) from late March to late October. The **US East Coast** (New York, Washington) uses UTC-5 in winter and UTC-4 from March to early November, when daylight saving time applies.
Client location
Their time vs Lagos in their summer
Their time vs Lagos in their winter
London (UK)
Same time as Lagos
1 hour behind Lagos
New York (US East)
5 hours behind Lagos
6 hours behind Lagos
Nairobi (Kenya, no clock change)
2 hours ahead all year
Accra (Ghana, no clock change)
1 hour behind all year
Let the calendar do the maths

In Google Calendar, check that your own time zone is set to Lagos (West Africa Time). When a client sends an invite, it will appear at the right local time. When you propose times, write both, for example '4pm WAT / 11am New York time', and double-check with a world clock app or a site such as timeanddate.com, especially in March, October and November when clocks change.
Finding the overlap

The **overlap** is the set of hours when both you and the client are normally working. Calls and quick questions should happen there. Everything else can be done **asynchronously**, which means you each work at different times and communicate in writing.
Worked example: overlap with a New York client in summer
Funke, for example, does virtual assistant work from Ibadan. A new client in New York works 9am to 5pm New York time and wants a short weekly call. It is July, so New York is 5 hours behind Lagos.
Convert the client's day to WAT: 9am + 5 hours = 2pm WAT; 5pm + 5 hours = 10pm WAT.
Funke's own working window is 9am to 6pm WAT, because evenings are for her children's homework.
Overlap = the hours inside both windows: 2pm to 6pm WAT, which is 9am to 1pm New York time.
She proposes 'Tuesdays at 3pm WAT / 10am New York time' for the weekly call.
She notes that in November, when New York moves to winter time, the same 3pm WAT becomes 9am New York time, and she will confirm with the client before the change.
Funke offers a call time that fits both days and has already planned for the clock change, which shows the client she is careful and organised.
A Lagos day with a New York client
9am WAT: focused solo work
2pm WAT: client day starts
3pm WAT: weekly call
6pm WAT: send end-of-day update
Evening: family, phone off
Solo work happens in the morning, contact happens in the overlap, and a written update closes the day.
Write your availability down

Clients relax when they know exactly when they can reach you. Put a short **availability statement** in your proposals, email signature or WhatsApp Business profile. Promise a **response time** you can keep every day, not your best day. Twenty-four hours on working days is common and reasonable for freelancers; a remote employer may set its own rule.
'Working hours: Monday to Friday, 9am to 6pm West Africa Time (UTC+1).'
'I reply to messages within one working day. For urgent issues during working hours, call or send a WhatsApp message marked URGENT.'
'I am not available on Sundays.'
Protecting your rest

Clients far away may message at your midnight. That does not mean you must reply at midnight. Turn on 'Do not disturb' for work apps after hours, and use WhatsApp Business away messages to tell people when you will reply. Steady, predictable replies build more trust than instant replies at every hour.
Plan the whole week, not only the calls

Time zones affect your week as well as your day. A client in the US may still be working on Friday evening in Lagos, and clients abroad have public holidays on different days from Nigeria's, so ask about theirs early. Block your week in a calendar: **focus blocks** for deep work at the hours you think best, **overlap blocks** for calls and quick replies, and **fixed family blocks** such as school runs and meals. Put deadlines in the calendar in the client's time zone and in yours, and plan to finish a day early. That spare day is what saves you when light or network fails.
Nigeria is on WAT (UTC+1) all year; the UK and US change clocks, so the gap changes.
Find the overlap hours and keep calls inside them; work asynchronously the rest of the time.
Always write both time zones when proposing a meeting.

Remote Delivery Standards: Tools, Communication and Getting Paid Safely

Remote clients judge you on what they can see: shared files, clear updates and work that arrives when promised. This module builds your remote toolkit, teaches the written communication habits of reliable remote workers, and shows how to receive money across borders without falling for scams.
The remote collaboration toolkit: shared files, task boards and video calls
Share Google Drive files with the correct permission level for each person
Use version history to recover or compare earlier work
Set up a simple task board with To do, Doing and Done lists
Run a short, well-prepared video call

In an office, a manager can walk to your desk and see what you are doing. In remote work, **your tools are your desk**. A client who can open one tidy shared folder, see a task board and join a call that starts on time will trust you quickly. You do not need expensive software. Free tools from Google and others are what many small teams use every day.
Two people working together on shared documents online
Shared files and boards let a client see progress without asking you for it.
Shared files with Google Drive
When you share a file or folder in Google Drive, you choose a **role** for each person. Choosing the right role protects the work.
Role
What the person can do
Use it for
Viewer
Open and read only
Final reports, invoices, portfolio samples
Commenter
Read and add comments or suggestions, but not change the text
Drafts you want feedback on
Editor
Change, add and delete content, and by default share it further
Team members who must work in the file with you

Share with the client's **named email address** where you can, rather than 'anyone with the link', because a link can be forwarded. For drafts, give the client **Commenter** access so their changes come as suggestions you can accept, and the original stays safe. In Google Docs, **Suggesting** mode (the pencil icon at the top) shows proposed edits in colour, which is ideal for proofreading jobs.
Version history: your safety net

Google Docs, Sheets and Slides save automatically. Open **File, then Version history, then See version history** to see earlier versions, who changed what, and to restore an older one. You can also **name a version**, for example 'Sent to client 12 May', so you can always show exactly what you delivered. If a client says 'you deleted my paragraph', version history settles it calmly.
A task board everyone can see

A **task board** turns a project into cards you move from left to right. Trello is a popular free tool for this; a simple Google Sheet with the same columns also works. Each card is one task with a due date and, if needed, a checklist.
How a task moves on the board
Backlog: agreed tasks
To do this week
Doing
Waiting for client

Anyone who opens the board can see what is finished, what is in progress and what is waiting on the client.
Worked example: setting up a project workspace
Chioma, for example, has won a one-month job writing 8 blog posts for a small dental clinic in Lagos. The clinic manager, Mr Bayo, wants to review drafts.
She creates a Drive folder 'Dental Clinic Blog 2026' with three sub-folders: Briefs, Drafts, Final.
She shares the main folder with Mr Bayo's email as Commenter, so he can suggest edits but cannot delete files.
She builds a Trello board with 8 cards, one per post, each with a due date: two posts a week.
She adds a 'Waiting for client' list so it is clear when a draft is with Mr Bayo, not with her.
When a post is approved, she moves the final copy into the Final folder, names the version 'Approved', and moves the card to Done.
Mr Bayo can see progress at any time without sending messages, and Chioma has a clear record of what was delivered and when.
Video calls that start well
Test the link, your microphone and your camera 10 minutes before. In Google Meet, the preview screen lets you check both.
Charge your device and close other apps that use data.
Sit facing a window or light, with a plain background. Use earphones to stop echo.
Send a short agenda before the call: three points and the decision you need.
Mute when you are not speaking, and keep to the time agreed.
After the call, send a written summary of decisions and next steps the same day.
Do not share more than you mean to

Before sharing your screen on a call, close personal chats, banking apps and other clients' files. Share one window instead of your whole screen where the app allows it. Never paste passwords into a shared document.

A simple rule ties this lesson together: **one home for every kind of information**. Files live in the shared folder, tasks live on the board, decisions live in writing. When a client asks 'where is it?', you should be able to answer with one link.
Use the client's tools when they have them

Larger clients and remote employers often already use their own tools, such as Slack for team chat, Microsoft Teams, Asana or Notion. Do not insist on yours. Ask in the first week: 'Which tools do you use for files, tasks and messages?' Most of these apps have free mobile versions and short help guides, and the skills carry over: a channel in Slack works like a WhatsApp group, a board in Asana works like Trello. Learn the basics in a day, set notifications for working hours only, and you will look like someone who has worked remotely for years.

Writing like a reliable remote worker: briefs, updates and handling delays
Confirm a brief in writing before starting work
Write a clear status update using Done, Next and Blockers
Warn a client about a delay early and offer options
Deliver work with a handover note that prevents confusion

In remote work, **most of your professionalism is written**. Your client may never see you, but they read every message. Remote teams often work **asynchronously**: people work at different times and rely on clear written messages instead of quick chats. This lesson gives you four message types that cover most of a project: the brief confirmation, the status update, the delay warning and the handover note.
Two people exchanging work messages on screens
Clear written messages replace the quick desk conversations remote teams cannot have.
1. Confirm the brief before you start

A **brief** is the description of the job. Clients often explain it loosely in a voice note or call. Before you start, write it back in a short message and ask them to confirm. This one habit prevents most arguments later.
**What** you will deliver (for example, 12 Instagram post designs in Canva, square size).
**By when**, with the time zone.
**How many revisions** are included.
**What you need from them** and by when (logo, photos, approvals).
**Price and payment terms**, if not already in a written agreement.
2. The status update: Done, Next, Blockers

A **blocker** is anything stopping you from moving forward, such as waiting for the client's photos. A short update on a fixed day, for example every Friday or at the end of each working day for a remote job, means the client never has to chase you.
A good status update
Done since last update
Next, with dates
Blockers and what you need
Any risk to the deadline
Link to the files
Five short lines answer every question a remote manager usually has.
Worked example: a Friday update
Grace, for example, manages Facebook and Instagram for a fashion brand owner in Abuja who travels a lot. She sends this update every Friday by 5pm WAT.
Done: 'Posted 5 of 5 planned posts this week. The Tuesday reel reached the most people so far.'
Next: 'Next week I will draft the 5 posts for the Sallah sale and send them to you on Tuesday for approval.'
Blockers: 'I need the new price list and 6 product photos by Monday, or the sale posts will be one day late.'
Risk: 'None if the photos arrive by Monday.'
Link: she pastes the link to the shared content calendar.
In under one minute of reading, the owner knows what happened, what is next, and exactly what Grace needs from her.
3. Warning about a delay
Delays happen. What damages trust is **silence**. Tell the client as soon as you see the risk, not on the deadline day. Say what happened in one sentence, without long excuses, and offer choices.
A delay message that keeps the client

'Hello Mrs Okafor, I want to warn you early: the power outage in my area since yesterday has slowed the video edit. I can either send the full video on Thursday instead of Wednesday, or send the first 60 seconds on Wednesday as planned and the rest on Thursday. Which do you prefer?'
4. The handover note

When you deliver, do not just send a file. A **handover note** lists what is included, where the files are, how to use them, and what happens next, such as the revision window. For example: 'Attached and in the Final folder: logo in PNG (for social media) and PDF (for printing). You have 2 rounds of revisions until 20 June. After that, changes are billed separately.'
Tone that works across cultures

Clients from different countries read tone differently. A safe style is **polite, short and specific**: a greeting, the main point first, one request per message, and a clear sign-off. Avoid long voice notes for clients abroad, because many cannot listen at work and they are hard to search later; send a written summary instead. Use the client's preferred name and title, and avoid slang or pidgin unless the client uses it first.

Keep important agreements **in writing on a channel you both use for work**, usually email for international clients. If something is agreed on a call or WhatsApp, follow up with a short email: 'As agreed on our call today...'. This becomes your record if there is ever a dispute about scope or payment.
Acknowledge every message, even before you have the answer

Remote clients worry most when a message seems to vanish. If you cannot answer fully, send a short **acknowledgement** within your stated response time: 'Received, thank you. I will check the figures and reply by 3pm WAT tomorrow.' Then keep that second promise. When a client sends several requests in one long message, reply with a numbered list that answers each point, so nothing is missed. Before sending any important message, read it once as if you were the client: is the main point in the first two lines, and is it clear what you need from them?

Send regular updates with Done, Next and Blockers so no one has to chase you.

Earning the money is only half the job. You also need to **receive it safely, in a form you can use**, and keep your accounts from being taken over. Payment options change often in Nigeria, so this lesson teaches you how to compare them and what questions to ask, rather than promising that any one service will always be best.
A person receiving a payment on a phone
Choose a payment route you can verify and withdraw from, before you start the work.

Before you accept any foreign client, check three things on the provider's **official website or app**: the current fees, whether the service works for Nigerian users right now, and how you withdraw to your local account. Ask in trusted freelancer communities what is working this month, but always confirm on the official site.
Know what you will actually receive
The price you quote is not the money that lands. Fees and exchange rates take a share. Always calculate your **net amount** before you agree a price.
Worked example: from invoice to naira
Zainab, for example, agrees a $300 project with a client in Canada, paid through a receiving service. The figures below are for practice only; she checks the real fees and rate on the day.
Invoice amount: $300.
Suppose the service charges a 1% receiving fee: $300 x 0.01 = $3, leaving $297.
Suppose she withdraws to her naira account at a rate of ₦1,450 per $1 and a 2% conversion margin is built into that rate. She receives $297 x ₦1,450 = ₦430,650.
She compares this with the open-market rate shown that day, for example ₦1,480: $297 x ₦1,480 = ₦439,560. The difference, ₦8,910, is the hidden cost of conversion.
Her real take-home is ₦430,650, which is about 97% of the full $300 at the higher rate.
Zainab now quotes knowing roughly 3% will go on fees and conversion, and she includes this in her price instead of being surprised.
Scams that target remote workers
Real client or scam?
Real client
Likely scam
Pays you for agreed work
Uses official company email or platform
Clear brief and named contact
Happy to sign a simple agreement
Asks you to pay a fee first
Sends 'overpayment', asks for refund
Moves you off the platform quickly
Pressure: 'decide today or lose it'
If any item on the right appears, stop and verify before you send money, documents or codes.
**Pay-to-work:** 'training fees', 'starter kits' or 'account activation' before you earn. Real employers do not charge you to be hired.

**Overpayment:** a 'client' sends more than agreed, often by a cheque or a transfer that is later reversed, and asks you to refund the difference. Wait until the money is cleared and confirmed by your bank, and refund only to the original source.
**Fake screenshot:** a payment 'receipt' image with no money in your account. Only trust your own bank or app balance.
**Off-platform pressure:** a marketplace client who wants to pay outside the platform. You lose the platform's payment protection, and it usually breaks the platform's rules.
**Task scams:** being paid small amounts to like videos or rate products, then asked to deposit money to 'unlock' bigger earnings.
Protect your accounts

Use a different strong password for your email, bank and work platforms, ideally a passphrase of four or more random words, kept in a password manager. Turn on 2-Step Verification on Google and on your freelance platforms, and set a WhatsApp two-step verification PIN. Never share a one-time code (OTP) with anyone, even someone who says they are from your bank or the platform's support team.

Finally, keep a simple **income record**: date, client, amount invoiced, fees, amount received in naira. It shows your true earnings, helps you price better and gives you evidence if a payment goes missing.

For new clients, protect yourself with **deposits and milestones**. Ask for part of the fee before you start, for example 50%, and the rest on delivery. For longer projects, split the work into stages and get paid for each stage before starting the next. On marketplaces, work only on contracts the platform has funded. If a client refuses any deposit on a first job, keep the first stage small so your risk is small too.

Growing Your Digital Enterprise: Remote Roles, Products and Community Impact

With your setup and standards in place, this module helps you grow: applying well for remote roles, adding a digital product or online shop as a second income stream, and launching your digital service with a 90-day plan that can also open doors for other women.
Finding and winning remote jobs and contract roles
Search for genuine remote roles using filters and reputable job boards
Tailor a CV and short cover note to a specific remote role
Prepare for a video interview and a paid or unpaid test task
Spot the warning signs of fake remote job offers

A remote job or longer contract gives the steady income that freelancing often lacks. Many Nigerian women now work as remote customer support agents, virtual assistants, content moderators, online tutors and project coordinators. The competition is real, so the women who succeed are usually not the most talented applicants. They are the ones who **apply precisely** and **show remote-work habits** from the first message.
A woman searching job listings on a large screen
A focused search with the right filters beats sending the same CV to hundreds of adverts.
Where to look

**LinkedIn Jobs:** search your role, then set the location type filter to 'Remote'. Read whether the role accepts applicants from Nigeria or only from certain countries; many adverts say this near the bottom.
**Remote-focused job boards** such as We Work Remotely and Remote OK, which list roles from companies that hire remotely.
**Company careers pages:** if you like a company, check its own website. Applying there avoids fake copies of the advert.
**Nigerian and African networks:** professional groups, alumni groups and women's networks often share remote roles from trusted members.
Read the location line

'Remote' does not always mean 'anywhere'. Some roles are 'Remote, US only' or 'Remote within Europe' because of tax and employment law. Applying to those wastes your time. Look for 'Remote (Worldwide)', 'Remote, Africa' or a time zone range such as 'UTC-1 to UTC+3', which includes Nigeria.
Tailor your CV for remote work

Many companies use an **applicant tracking system (ATS)**, software that scans CVs for the skills listed in the advert. Use the advert's own words for skills you genuinely have, keep the layout simple (no tables or text inside pictures), and save it as a PDF unless told otherwise. Add a short line that proves remote readiness.
Worked example: tailoring one CV to one advert

Joy, for example, from Port Harcourt, finds a remote 'Customer Support Associate' role open to applicants in Africa. The advert asks for written English, experience with Zendesk or similar tools, and availability 2pm to 10pm WAT.
She highlights the advert's key words: written communication, ticketing system, customer satisfaction, evening shift.
She rewrites her retail job line from 'Attended to customers' to 'Resolved about 40 customer enquiries a day in person and on WhatsApp, keeping a written log of every complaint'.
She adds the free Freshdesk tutorial she completed under Skills, describing it honestly as 'self-taught, practice account'.
She adds a 'Remote setup' line: 'Laptop, headset, two internet providers, power backup; available 2pm to 10pm WAT.'
She writes a 5-sentence cover note that names the company, the role and one specific reason she fits, and she checks every sentence for spelling.
Joy sends one carefully matched application instead of twenty generic ones, and her CV now answers the employer's main remote questions before they ask.
What gets you hired remotely
Proof of results
Clear written English
Remote setup and availability
Matching skills from the advert
Matching skills gets you past the scan; setup, writing and real results win the interview.
Interviews and test tasks

Remote interviews happen on video. Use the call checklist from Module 2, and prepare short stories using **STAR**: the Situation, the Task, the Action you took and the Result. Expect remote-specific questions: 'How do you manage your time without supervision?', 'Tell us about a problem with your internet and how you handled it', 'How do you keep a manager updated?'. Your answers from this course, such as your backup plan and update routine, are exactly what they want to hear.

Many employers set a **test task**, such as answering three sample customer emails. A short test is normal. A long task that looks like real work for their business, such as writing ten full articles, is not; ask whether it is paid, or offer a shorter sample. Never send original files you have not been paid for without a watermark or a limited preview.

Keep a simple **application tracker**: company, role, link, date applied, contact person, stage and next action. Follow up once, politely, about a week after the closing date if you have heard nothing. Rejections are normal in remote hiring, even for strong candidates, so judge yourself by the quality of each application and keep going. After every interview, write down the questions you were asked; your answers get sharper each time.
Signs of a fake remote job

Be very careful if the 'interview' happens only by text chat on Telegram or WhatsApp, if you are offered the job without any real interview, if they send you a cheque to buy equipment from 'their supplier', or if they ask for your BVN, bank login or OTP. Check that the recruiter's email uses the company's own domain and that the job also appears on the company's real website.
Use the Remote filter and remote job boards, and read which countries a role accepts.

Adding a second stream: digital products and selling online
Choose a digital product idea that grows from your existing service
Calculate the price and break-even number of sales for a digital product
Calculate profit per order for a physical product sold online
Respect copyright and licence rules when creating products

Once your first income model is working, a **second stream** protects you when clients are quiet. The best second stream grows from what you already do. A bookkeeper can sell a spreadsheet template; a caterer who already sells online can sell a recipe e-book; a social media manager can sell a 30-day content planner. This lesson covers both digital products and selling physical goods online, with the numbers that tell you whether each idea is worth it.
A person browsing and buying products in an online shop
An online shop or product page can earn while you sleep, but only if the numbers work.
Digital products that suit service providers
Your service
Possible product
Format
Bookkeeping or virtual assistance
Monthly cash book and budget template
Google Sheets or Excel file with instructions
Graphic design
Editable flyer templates for churches or events
Canva template link or design files
Teaching or tutoring
WAEC or Common Entrance practice packs
PDF workbook with answers
Catering
Small chops costing guide and recipes
PDF e-book with a costing sheet

You can sell from a WhatsApp catalogue with a payment link, or use a platform built for digital products, such as Selar, which was started in Nigeria, or Gumroad. These platforms deliver the file automatically after payment. Compare their fees and payout options on their official sites before choosing.

A good digital product page answers four questions in plain words: **who it is for**, **what problem it solves**, **exactly what the buyer gets** (number of pages, file type, whether it works on a phone), and **how to use it** after download. Add two or three clear screenshots, and a short video if you can. Include simple instructions inside the file too, because a buyer who cannot open or use the product will ask for a refund or never buy again. Decide your refund rule before launch and state it on the page.
Worked example: pricing a template and finding break-even
Ruth, for example, is a bookkeeper in Abeokuta. She wants to sell a 'Small Shop Cash Book' Google Sheets template to market women and small shop owners.
Her costs to create it: about 20 hours of her time, which she values at ₦2,500 an hour (20 x ₦2,500 = ₦50,000), plus about ₦15,000 for a short promotion. Total cost: ₦65,000.
She checks similar templates and sets her price at ₦4,000 (approximate, market-tested).
Suppose the selling platform keeps about 10% per sale: ₦4,000 x 0.10 = ₦400, so she keeps ₦3,600.
Break-even sales = total cost ÷ amount kept per sale = ₦65,000 ÷ ₦3,600 = 18.06, so 19 sales.
Every sale after the 19th is profit, with no extra cost of stock.
Ruth knows she must sell 19 copies to recover her time and promotion money, and she can now set a realistic goal, such as 30 sales in three months through her existing clients and WhatsApp status.
Service feeds product, product feeds service
Do client work
Notice repeated questions

More client work
Products built from real client problems sell better, and buyers often become service clients.
Selling physical goods online: count every naira
For physical products, profit per order must cover the item, packaging, payment fees and any delivery cost you absorb. Many online sellers lose money because they forget packaging or free delivery.
Add up the cost of one item: materials or buying price, plus packaging and label. For example, a jar of whipped shea butter: ₦1,800 ingredients + ₦600 jar and label = ₦2,400.
Add any cost you pay per order, such as a payment fee of about ₦100 and ₦300 towards delivery: ₦2,400 + ₦400 = ₦2,800.
Subtract from the selling price. At ₦4,500: ₦4,500 - ₦2,800 = ₦1,700 profit per jar.
Check the margin: ₦1,700 ÷ ₦4,500 = about 38%. If a promotion cuts the price to ₦3,500, profit falls to ₦700, so plan discounts carefully.
Copyright and licences

Only sell what you have the right to sell. Do not copy other people's e-books, photos, recipes written word-for-word, past exam papers that belong to an exam body, or brand logos. If you build templates with Canva or stock photos, read the platform's licence: some elements may be used in your own designs but not resold as stand-alone templates. Food and cosmetic products may also need NAFDAC registration before wider sale.

Start small: one product, one clear buyer, one channel. Test it with ten people you already know, ask what confused them, improve it, then promote it. A product that ten buyers recommend is a better foundation than ten products no one has tested.

For physical goods, include packaging, payment fees and delivery in cost per order.

Launching your digital service, a 90-day plan and lifting other women
Assemble a launch kit: offer, work sample, availability and payment route
Set a 90-day plan with weekly activity targets and checkpoints
Handle client and team data in line with Nigeria's data protection law
Plan one way to share skills or work with other women

This final lesson brings everything together into a **launch**: the day you start actively offering your digital service, with a plan for the next 90 days. Your capstone project for this course is built from the work you do here, so keep everything you create.
A rocket launching to show the start of a new venture
Launch day is the start of steady weekly action, not a single big announcement.
Your launch kit
**Offer line:** who you help, with what, and the result. For example: 'I manage Instagram pages for Abuja bakeries so they post 4 times a week without stress.'
**Work sample or portfolio:** 2 to 3 pieces, real or clearly labelled as practice samples.
**Availability statement** with time zone and response time (Module 1).
**Workspace templates:** shared folder, task board and your four message templates (Module 2).
**Payment route** checked on the official site, and your income record sheet (Module 2).
**Outreach list** of at least 20 named, suitable businesses or adverts.
The 90-day plan: activity you control

You cannot control whether a client says yes. You can control **how many good-quality approaches you make** and how well you follow up. Set targets for activity, then check results every 30 days and adjust.

Turn the 90-day target into a **weekly routine** you can keep alongside home duties. For example: Monday, research 5 new prospects; Tuesday and Wednesday, send 10 personal approaches; Thursday, follow up on last week's messages; Friday, update your tracker and portfolio. Ten approaches a week is about 40 a month. Protect paid client work first: if a busy week of delivery leaves no time for outreach, note it and catch up the next week rather than abandoning the plan. Write your three main measures at the top of your tracking sheet: approaches sent, replies, paid jobs.
Your first 90 days
Days 1-30: launch, 40 approaches
Day 30: review, adjust offer
Days 31-60: 40 approaches, deliver well
Day 60: ask for testimonials
Days 61-90: repeat clients, raise rates
Each 30-day block ends with a review so the next block uses what you learned.
Worked example: reading 30-day results
Blessing, for example, offers CV writing and LinkedIn profile setup from Jos. In her first 30 days she tracked everything in a simple sheet.
She sent 40 personal approaches: 25 on LinkedIn, 15 through WhatsApp contacts.
She got 8 replies: 8 ÷ 40 = 20% reply rate.
3 of the 8 became paid jobs: 3 ÷ 8 = 37.5% of replies converted, or 3 ÷ 40 = 7.5% of all approaches.
All 3 paying clients came from WhatsApp contacts; LinkedIn brought 5 replies but no sales yet.
Decision for days 31 to 60: keep 40 approaches, but send 25 through referrals and WhatsApp, rewrite her LinkedIn message to include a before-and-after sample, and ask each client for a referral.
Instead of feeling that 'LinkedIn does not work', Blessing has numbers that show where her clients come from and one specific thing to change.
Handle personal data responsibly

Remote work often means handling other people's personal data: customer lists, CVs, phone numbers, ID cards. Nigeria's **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023**, overseen by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC), sets rules for how personal data is collected and used. For a small digital business, good practice includes:
Collect only the data you need for the job, and say what you will use it for.
Keep client files in your protected cloud folder, not in open WhatsApp groups.
Never reuse one client's customer list for another client or for your own marketing.
Delete or return personal data when the job ends, unless the client agrees otherwise.
Tell the client at once if their data may have been exposed, for example if your phone is stolen.
Lifting other women

Digital work can grow beyond one person. As you gain clients, you may need help with overflow work, and other women need a first opportunity. You can train one woman in your skill, refer clients you cannot take, or form a small team where one person handles design and another handles writing. If you subcontract, agree the task, deadline, quality standard and pay in writing, pay promptly, and remain responsible to your client for the final quality. Check each piece before it goes to the client, and do not share the client's private information with a helper unless the client has agreed. Some women in the WODDI network may also be ready to form a small digital cooperative or study group: meeting online once a week to share leads, review each other's portfolios and practise interviews costs little and keeps everyone moving.
Share honestly

When you share your story with other women, include the real numbers and the slow weeks, not only the wins. An honest account of '40 messages, 3 clients' helps a beginner far more than a screenshot of one big payment.

This is the video for module 1 of Digital Entrepreneurship and Remote Work.
Four different businesses
Four ways to earn online
Remote job: one employer, steady salary
Freelancing: many clients, uneven income
E-commerce: real goods sold online
Digital products: make once, sell many times
People say make money online as if it were one thing. It is not. There are four models, and each pays, grows and fails differently.
A remote job means working for one organisation from home. The income is predictable, but the employer sets your hours and tasks, and competition is strong.
A freelancer sells a service to several clients, by project or on a retainer, which is a fixed monthly fee for ongoing work. You choose your clients, but income goes up and down.
E-commerce means selling physical goods online. You need money for stock, and you still pack and deliver. The internet widens your market, but it does not remove the work of a shop.
A digital product, like a budget template or a recipe e-book, is made once and sold many times. But sales start slowly, because people must first find and trust you.
Worked example
How Ngozi chose her starting model
List skills and honest hours: about 15 a week
Rule out e-commerce: no money for stock
Rule out a full-time job: hours clash
Choose freelancing first: editing documents
Keep a template pack as a later second stream
For example, Ngozi is a teacher in Enugu with two children. She writes clearly and uses Google Docs well, and can spare about 15 hours a week.
She has no money or space for stock, so e-commerce waits.
Her teaching hours clash with a 9am to 5pm job, so that is out too.
She chooses freelancing, editing and proofreading documents, because it can bring money within weeks.
And she writes down a lesson-plan template pack as a later idea. One model now, a second one planned.
Be careful of offers that promise big daily earnings for simple online tasks, or ask for an activation fee. Real employers and clients pay you. They do not charge you to start.
Measure, then budget
Amina's monthly data budget
One work week on the data screen: 3.2 GB
Four weeks: 3.2 x 4 = 12.8 GB
Add 25% for extra calls: 12.8 x 1.25 = 16 GB
Choose a plan of at least 16 GB
Keep a small top-up on a second SIM
Guessing your data use means running out in the middle of a client call. So measure it on your phone's data usage screen.
For example, Amina manages social media for two businesses from Kano. Her work apps used 3.2 GB in one ordinary week.
Four weeks of the same work is 12.8 GB.
She adds about 25% as a safety margin. That makes 16 GB.
She picks a plan of at least 16 GB and keeps a small top-up on her second SIM. She writes data in her records each month as a business cost, like transport.
Backup plan
When light or network fails
Phone, laptop and power bank charged before every big call or deadline.
Use two networks. When one is weak, switch your hotspot to the other.
Turn on offline access in Google Docs. Keep client files in Google Drive with 2-Step Verification.
A client abroad does not see NEPA or a weak network. They only see late work. So charge everything the night before an important call or deadline.
Use two SIMs on different networks, so you can switch when one is weak.
Turn on offline access in Google Docs, and save client work in a cloud folder, not only on your phone. Protect that account with 2-Step Verification.
And if a problem is coming, message the client before the deadline, not after.
Electricity safety
Keep your equipment and home safe
Surge protector or stabiliser for laptops
Do not overload one extension socket
Cables away from water and children
Unplug during heavy lightning storms

Power often returns with a surge, so use a surge protector or stabiliser. Do not overload one extension socket. Keep cables away from water and from where children walk. And switch off and unplug during heavy lightning storms.
Time zones
Finding the overlap with a client
Nigeria is WAT, UTC+1, all year
New York in July: 5 hours behind Lagos
Client's 9am to 5pm = 2pm to 10pm WAT
Overlap with 9am to 6pm WAT: 2pm to 6pm
Propose: 3pm WAT / 10am New York time
A meeting at 3pm means nothing until you know whose 3pm. Nigeria uses West Africa Time, UTC plus 1, and never changes its clocks. The UK and the US do.
For example, Funke is a virtual assistant in Ibadan. Her new client is in New York, which in July is 5 hours behind Lagos.
The client works 9am to 5pm. Add 5 hours, and that is 2pm to 10pm in Lagos.
Funke works 9am to 6pm, because evenings are for her children. The overlap, the hours inside both days, is 2pm to 6pm.
So she proposes 3pm WAT, 10am New York time, always writing both. She also notes that in November the gap changes, and confirms with the client before then.
Key points
Remember
Start with one model that fits your hours and money
Measure data for a week, times 4, plus a margin
Two SIMs, a power bank and offline mode
Write both time zones when proposing a meeting
Publish hours and a reply time you can keep
To remember. Pick one model that fits your life now. Budget your data from real numbers. Keep backups for power and internet.
Always write both time zones. And publish your working hours with a reply time you can keep every day, for example within one working day.

Deliver remotely, write clearly, and get paid safely
Deliver remotely, write clearly, and get paid safely.
This is the video for module 2: Remote Delivery Standards, Tools, Communication and Getting Paid Safely.
Why this matters
Clients judge what they can see
Your tools are your desk
Most of your professionalism is written
The price you quote is not what lands
Scammers target remote workers
In an office, a manager can walk to your desk. In remote work, your tools are your desk: one tidy shared folder, a task board, a call that starts on time.
Your client may never see you, but they read every message.
And getting paid is only half the job. You must receive the money safely, and keep scammers out of your accounts.
Google Drive
Give the smallest role they need
Open and read only. For final reports, invoices and portfolio samples.
Can suggest and comment, but not change the text. Best for client drafts.
Can change, delete and share further. Only for team members working in the file.
When you share in Google Drive, you choose a role. A Viewer can only open and read.

A Commenter can suggest changes but not alter your text. Give clients this for drafts, so the original stays safe. Share to their named email, not anyone with the link, because a link can be forwarded.
An Editor can change and delete, so keep that for people who must work in the file.
And if a client says you deleted their paragraph, open File, then Version history. It shows who changed what, calmly.
Worked example
Grace's Friday update
Done: posted 5 of 5 planned posts
Next: draft 5 Sallah sale posts by Tuesday
Blockers: need price list and 6 photos by Monday
Risk: none if photos arrive Monday
Link: the shared content calendar
For example, Grace manages social media for a fashion brand owner in Abuja who travels a lot. Every Friday by 5pm she sends a short update, so the owner never has to chase her.
Done. What she finished this week.
Next. What she will do, with dates.
Blockers. A blocker is anything stopping you, like waiting for the client's photos. She says exactly what she needs and by when.
Then any risk to the deadline, and a link to the files. In under one minute, the owner knows everything.
When things go wrong
Warning about a delay
Delays happen. What damages trust is silence.
Warn as soon as you see the risk
Say what happened in one sentence
Offer the client two choices
Confirm call or WhatsApp agreements by email
Tell the client as soon as you see a risk, not on the deadline day.
Explain in one sentence, without long excuses. For example, a power outage has slowed the video edit.
Then offer choices: the full video on Thursday, or the first 60 seconds on Wednesday as planned and the rest on Thursday. Which do you prefer?
And when something is agreed on a call, follow up with a short email: as agreed on our call today. That becomes your record.
Know your net amount
From a dollar invoice to naira
For example, Zainab invoices a client in Canada $300. Practice figures only.
Received at 1,450 per $1
Same at the 1,480 market rate
Hidden cost of conversion
Practice figures. Check real fees and rates.
The price you quote is not the money that lands. Suppose the receiving service charges 1%. That is $3, leaving $297.
She withdraws at 1,450 naira per dollar, and receives 430,650 naira.
At the open-market rate that day, 1,480, it would be 439,560.
So 8,910 naira was a hidden cost of conversion. Her take-home is about 97% of the full $300.
Now she prices knowing roughly 3% goes on fees. Always check the real fees on the provider's official website on the day.
Stop and verify
Official email or platform
Clear brief, named contact
Happy to sign an agreement
Overpays, asks for a refund
Moves you off the platform
Pressure: decide today
A real client pays you for agreed work, uses an official email or platform, and is happy to sign a simple agreement.
A scammer asks you to pay first, or sends too much and asks for a refund before the money has cleared. Refund only after your bank confirms it, and only to the original source.
Never trust a screenshot. Only trust your own bank or app balance.
Protect your money
Your account safety checklist
A different strong password for each account
2-Step Verification on Google and platforms
A WhatsApp two-step PIN
Never share a one-time code (OTP)
New clients: a deposit, for example 50%
Use a different strong password for your email, bank and work platforms. Turn on 2-Step Verification, and set a WhatsApp two-step PIN.
Never share a one-time code, even with someone who says they are from your bank. And with new clients, ask for part of the fee before you start, for example 50%.
Key points
Remember
Smallest Drive role; version history as proof
Updates: Done, Next, Blockers
Warn about delays early, with options
Calculate your net amount before pricing
Never pay to work, never share an OTP

To remember. Share with the smallest role. Send regular updates so no one chases you. Warn about delays early. Know your net amount before you agree a price. And never pay to get work, or share a code.

Win remote roles, add a second stream, launch in 90 days
Win remote roles, add a second income stream, and launch your service in 90 days.
This is the video for module 3: Growing Your Digital Enterprise.
Finding genuine remote roles
LinkedIn Jobs with the Remote filter
Remote job boards like We Work Remotely
The company's own careers page
Trusted Nigerian and women's networks
A remote job gives the steady income freelancing often lacks. The women who win are usually not the most talented. They apply precisely, and show remote-work habits from the first message.
On LinkedIn Jobs, set the location filter to Remote.
Try remote job boards such as We Work Remotely and Remote OK.
Check the company's own careers page, which avoids fake copies of the advert.
And use trusted networks. Then read the location line. Remote, US only, is not open to you. Look for Remote, Worldwide, or Remote, Africa.
Worked example
Joy tailors one CV to one advert
One carefully matched application beats twenty generic ones.
Highlight the advert's key skill words
Rewrite duties as results: 40 enquiries a day
Add true skills, honestly described
Add a remote setup line with hours
A 5-sentence cover note, spelling checked
For example, Joy in Port Harcourt finds a remote customer support role open to applicants in Africa. Many companies use software that scans CVs for the advert's words, so she highlights them.
Attended to customers becomes: resolved about 40 customer enquiries a day, keeping a written log of every complaint.
She adds a free tutorial she completed, honestly described as self-taught.
She adds a remote setup line: laptop, headset, two internet providers, power backup, available 2pm to 10pm WAT.
Then a 5-sentence cover note that names the company and one reason she fits. One precise application, not twenty generic ones.
Protect yourself
Real job or fake job?
Real remote job
A real video interview
Recruiter uses the company domain
Job is on the company website
A short test task
Fake job
Text-only chat on Telegram
Offered a job with no interview
A cheque to buy equipment
Asks for BVN, bank login or OTP
A real employer interviews you on video, and the job also appears on the company's own website. A short test task is normal. A long one that looks like real unpaid work is not.

Be very careful if the interview happens only by text on Telegram or WhatsApp, if you get the job with no real interview, or if they send a cheque to buy equipment. Never give your BVN, bank login or OTP.
A second stream
Ruth finds her break-even point
For example, Ruth is a bookkeeper in Abeokuta selling a cash book template.
20 hours of her time at 2,500
A short promotion
Naira prices are approximate.
A second stream protects you when clients are quiet, and the best one grows from what you already do. Ruth makes a Google Sheets cash book for small shop owners.
She values 20 hours of her time at 2,500 naira an hour, which is 50,000, and spends 15,000 on promotion.
Her total cost is 65,000 naira. She prices the template at 4,000. The platform keeps about 10%, so she keeps 3,600 per sale.
Break-even is total cost divided by what she keeps: 65,000 divided by 3,600 is 18.06. So she needs 19 sales. Every sale after that is profit.
Read your numbers
Blessing's first 30 days
40 personal approaches sent
8 replies: a 20% reply rate
3 paid jobs, all from WhatsApp contacts
Next: more referrals, a better LinkedIn message
You cannot control whether a client says yes. You can control how many good approaches you make. For example, Blessing offers CV writing from Jos, and tracks everything.
In 30 days she sent 40 personal approaches.
She got 8 replies. That is a 20% reply rate.
3 became paid jobs, and all 3 came from WhatsApp contacts. LinkedIn brought replies but no sales yet.
So instead of saying LinkedIn does not work, she changes one thing: more referrals, and a LinkedIn message with a before-and-after sample.
Personal data
Handle client data responsibly
Never reuse one client's customer list for anyone else.
Collect only the data you need
Keep files in your protected cloud folder
Delete or return data when the job ends
Tell the client at once if data is exposed
Remote work often means handling CVs, phone numbers and customer lists. The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 sets rules for this. Collect only what you need.
Keep files in your protected cloud folder, not in open WhatsApp groups.
Delete or return personal data when the job ends.
Tell the client at once if their data may be exposed, for example if your phone is stolen. And never reuse one client's list for another client or your own marketing.
Three ways to share the work
Teach your skill to one woman who needs a first opportunity.
Pass on clients you cannot take to women you trust.
One handles design, another writing. Agree task, deadline, quality and pay in writing.
As you grow, other women need a first opportunity. You can train one woman in your skill.
You can refer clients you cannot take.
Or form a small team. Agree the task, deadline, quality and pay in writing, pay promptly, and check every piece yourself, because you stay responsible to your client.
Key points
Remember
Apply precisely; read the location line
Never give BVN, bank login or OTP
Break-even = total cost ÷ amount kept per sale
Set activity targets; review every 30 days
Protect client data; lift other women

To remember. Apply precisely to roles open to you, and walk away from fake jobs. Work out break-even before you build a product. Count your approaches and review every 30 days. And protect client data as you bring other women along.
